provenance: Opus 5.5 subscription CLI draft with host review/repairs, source restrictions and execution verification.

draft_notes.explanation: Canonically, the input is a 3-row strip holding colour pieces. Each piece is a 4-connected same-colour component and a slice of a monotone snake path. Gap columns separate the pieces, and each piece has been shifted vertically. The output removes every gap and restores the snake. Pieces keep their order along the long axis, and the first piece stays anchored at the starting edge. Each later piece is placed directly after the previous one. It is shifted across the strip so that its near end sits in the same cross-row as the previous piece's far end. A piece's end in a boundary line is the cell in that line with the fewest same-piece 4-neighbours, which is the path tip. The factory works out where the canonical directions point after the D4 transform. Vectors are flipped as (dr,dc)->(dr,-dc) when d4>=4, then rotated clockwise as (dr,dc)->(dc,-dr), d4%4 times. From this it derives three constants. A is the visible axis that carries the chain order (columns or rows). SIGN says whether the chain starts at the low or the high edge of that axis. CS is the visible direction of canonical increasing row, used only for the deterministic tie-break. The background is the constant palette[0]. The emitted program works entirely in visible coordinates. It finds the components and orders them from the start edge along axis A. The output length along A is the sum of the piece extents, and the cross size is unchanged. When SIGN is -1, pieces are packed from the far output edge, so the first piece stays anchored where it already is. Every piece is translated along A and across C, with no rotation of the grid and no colour remapping.
draft_notes.limitations: This has not been executed; the host must verify it. The end-cell rule uses the fewest-neighbours tip, with ties broken by the canonical-row direction, as in the archived solver. In the constructor's random domain no ties occur. Only the first run can have length 2, and runs after it are 3-5 long (an optional final run of 1 shares its column with a connector). So no two connector columns are adjacent and no 2x2 blocks appear. Fixture pair 3 uses a final run of length 2, outside the random sampler's range. It still produces no tie. Colour 0 (palette[0]) is assumed to be the background; the constructor always uses a zero-filled canvas and random_color for pieces. A piece whose colour equals the background, or two touching pieces of the same colour, would break component extraction. Neither can occur because gap columns always separate pieces. Cells pushed outside the output by an inconsistent shift are clipped, as in the archive; this does not happen in the domain. No contradictions between the fixtures and the uniform rule were found by reading them. No constructor defect affects the visible rule. The bump column only adds a trailing blank line at the far end and is ignored naturally.

independent_source_review.mechanism: The constructor draws a monotone left-to-right snake on a 3-row output. Horizontal runs sit at rows hrows, and each vertical connector lies in the shared last column of the previous run. It then cuts the output columns into consecutive pieces of width vlengths, gives each piece a vertical offset voffset (with voffset[0]=0), and places the pieces in the input separated by one gap column, plus an optional trailing bump column. The solver reverses this. It extracts same-colour 4-components and orders them along the chain axis. It packs them with no gaps, keeps the first piece's cross position, and shifts each later piece across the strip. The shift puts its near-end tip, the cell with the fewest same-piece neighbours in its near boundary line, in the same cross-line as the previous piece's far-end tip.
evidence: The input hides only the voffsets, and each one can be recovered from visible geometry. In the output, the path crosses from column c to column c+1 at exactly one row. That row is the right end of piece k and the left end of piece k+1. A rigid shift of each piece therefore recovers the output exactly.

Tip correctness when the piece's far boundary is a connector column. The column holds a vertical segment from last_row to hrow, at least 2 cells because hrows excludes a repeat of the previous row. The last_row cell has a left neighbour plus a vertical neighbour (degree 2), and the hrow cell has only a vertical neighbour inside the piece (degree 1). So the exit cell is the unique minimum.

Tip correctness when the piece's near boundary is a connector column. This is the mirror case: the entry cell at last_row has degree 1, and the exit cell has a right neighbour plus a vertical neighbour (degree 2). The case where both boundaries of a width-2 piece are connectors also resolves uniquely.

No degree ties are reachable. Only the first run may have length 2, and later runs are 3-5. A final run of length 1 reuses the previous run's last column. So connector columns are never adjacent and no 2x2 blocks form. The CS tie-break is therefore never decisive.

Each output column contains at least one path cell, so every piece's visible extent equals vlength, and total = sum(vlengths) = outwidth. The sampler enforces this equality (sum(vlengths) != outwidth -> continue). The validate() fixtures also satisfy it, for example pair 1 gives 3+3+3 = 11-3+1 = 9 and pair 3 gives 3+2+3 = 8.
Pieces are always separated by a gap column (in_column += 1), so equal random colours cannot merge components. random_color draws from 1..9, so no piece uses the background colour.

voffsets[0]=0 means the first piece is genuinely anchored, which is a visible rule taught by every demonstration. The bump column becomes a trailing or leading blank line and is ignored, because placement depends only on piece positions.

Factory D4 handling. The constants come from the canonical along vector (0,1) and cross vector (1,0), mapped by flip then clockwise rotation. When SIGN=-1 the solver packs from the far output edge (target=total-1-cur, near=hi), which matches where the first piece lies after reversal. The solver works directly in visible coordinates and does not wrap an untransform around the whole grid.

Host audit passed 1000 fresh pairs and 8000 augmented checks, which suggests all 8 D4 variants, plus 16 fixture variants. This is consistent with the factory's flip-then-rotate convention matching the host.
nonblocking_limits: The CS tie-break and the out-of-bounds clipping branch are defensive only. The constructor domain never exercises them.
BG is hard-coded as palette[0] instead of being inferred. This is valid because the constructor always uses a zero canvas and non-zero piece colours.
The degree-based tip rule depends on structural properties of the constructor: no adjacent connector columns and no 2x2 blocks. Inputs outside that domain could tie.
Correctness of the orientation constants depends on the host using the same D4 convention (flip, then clockwise rotation). The host's augmented checks support this but do not prove it in general.
